This is my story…⬇️

My name is Elise. 

I didn’t come from a wealthy family. 

I was the child of a single immigrant father and a mother who passed away when I was 9 years old.

My high school lacked the guidance I needed for the college admissions process. 

But one thing I learned is that your background does NOT define you. Your determination does🌟

So after pushing myself even when it felt impossible, staying up late perfecting my essays, and spending hundreds of hours understanding what colleges look for, I graduated valedictorian and received ZERO Ivy League rejections 🏆

I’m now pursuing a degree in Molecular & Cellular Biology + Global Health & Health Policy (Pre-Med track) at Harvard University, and I’ve been featured in Forbes Magazine as the founder of Ultimate Ivy League Guide.

I’ve guided millions of students through the college admissions process, and now continue to help students apply to top schools like Harvard, Yale, Cornell, Stanford, Columbia, University of California campuses, and more 📚

My purpose is to empower as many students as possible. This is why I created my Ultimate Mentor program 💪

As the first step to fulfilling my purpose I put together a mass document of 50+ FREE college admission courses so just comment “MENTOR” and I’ll send it to you 😊

#UltimateIvyLeagueGuide #UltimateMentor #Mentor #UILG

HOW IMPORTANT ARE GRADES TO ADMISSION OFFICERS? 👀⬇️

The truth is: High grades will NOT set you apart.

If two applicants have the exact same grades, SAT score, and background, what will differentiate them is their:

1. Potential for future success
2. Application strategy

So how can you ensure you’re doing the right things?

Well, to be honest, there isn’t a cookie cutter strategy that will secure your acceptance.

But what IS NECESSARY is understanding the overall framework and KEY MILESTONES to focus on during your high school years.

After receiving ZERO Ivy League rejections and now at the top 5% of my class at Harvard University, I realized that the college admission process is a level playing field as long as you have a GENUINE passion and the right mentor to guide you through the complex admissions process 🌟

I’ve since helped millions of students avoid the initial mistakes I made and secure acceptances into their dream schools 🏆📚

I want to help YOU.

So if you want all 13 of my free college admission guides + access to 5 courses from my flagship program, just comment “MENTOR” and I’ll send it to you:) ❤️

The difference between a strong and weak interview answer is specificity ⬇️

❌ Why the Rejected Answer Doesn’t Work: “Prestige” and “dream school” describe nothing Yale can picture. There’s no reason it had to be Yale, no thing I would actually do there, and no connection to anything I have already done. My interviewer walks away without learning a single thing about me.

✅ Why the Accepted Answer Works: It starts with something I have really been doing, names the exact problem I keep running into, and points at one specific thing at Yale I would join to fix it. That signals direction, self-awareness, and a reason it had to be this school.

Top schools score you using specific rubrics…👇

At a school like Harvard, you’re scored from 1 to 6 on your academics, your extracurriculars, your personal qualities, and even your teachers’ letters.

Meanwhile, Yale has multiple officers read your file and rate your profile before anyone votes.

And your score isn’t an average of all of it. It leans toward whatever you’re strongest at.

Which is why the students who stand out are usually the ones who let one real strength carry their whole application, instead of trying to do a little of everything.

Once I understood that, it shaped the classes I took, the activities I stuck with, and the way I wrote my essays.

I know you’re probably thinking, “That’s easy for you to say Elise.”

Yes, I got into Harvard, built a collective following of 2M+, was featured on Forbes, and invited to speak at multiple Harvard conferences.

But honestly, when I was 16, I wanted all of that because I wanted other people to validate that I was worth something…

What I figured out when I reached these goals is that the moments I actually cared about had nothing to do with any of it. 

They were the times I got to show up for someone, or build something that positively impacted the people around me. 

That’s when I understood that what matters most to me is community and service, and that none of it was going to mean much until it was focused at something bigger than myself.

So I’ve stopped measuring my life by the goals I set at 16.

I’m proud of that girl and everything she worked for…

But I’m chasing something different now, and it doesn’t depend on tangible success or anyone else’s approval.

My mission for @ultimateivyleagueguide was never just about getting into college. It’s about helping students see everything they’re capable of, and walking them through a process that feels scary so they never have to face it alone ❤️

Most students think a “Why This Major?” essay is about how much you love the subject 😬

The thing that actually separates a rejected, waitlisted, and accepted answer is your trajectory.

Here’s why each response got its result:

❌ Rejected: Leans on clichés about the field. It’s the future, there’s so much opportunity, and I’ve always loved it….every single applicant to the major could write the same lines.

⚠️ Waitlisted: Shows real interest and a bit of research, naming AI and a class or two. The answer still sits in the abstract, with plenty about what the field offers and not much about the student’s own work.

✅ Accepted: Connects three things: something the student already built, the insight she pulled from it, and where she’ll take it next. The major becomes the next step in a story that’s already moving.

Most students put their essay at the center of their application strategy…

Application season opens in one week, and most students are about to spend it working on the wrong thing.

#ultimateivyleagueguide #ultimatementor #uilg

There’s a reason why these answers have different outcomes…and it all comes down to institutional priorities and fit:

✅ACCEPTED: This student started with something they already did, then shows how a specific Harvard opportunity helps them think more carefully about impact before scaling it beyond their own community. That signals judgment, responsibility, and direction, which are three values Harvard cares deeply about.

⚠️WAITLISTED: This student understands Harvard’s values, but they stays aspirational. It’s not enough to talk about growth and impact without grounding those goals in lived experience or showing why Harvard is the necessary next step.

❌REJECTED: This student focuses on Harvard’s reputation and resources. That tells admissions what the school can offer the student, not what the student is already doing or how they would contribute.

- - - 

If you want to write an admitted-level “Why Harvard,” do this:

1️⃣ Start with something concrete you have already done that involved responsibility, leadership, or systems-level issues.

2️⃣Name one real Harvard program, course, or pathway that directly sharpens how you think or act in that area.

3️⃣Show how Harvard is the logical next step to deepen your judgment before expanding your impact beyond your own community.

Most students think a “community” essay is about naming a group and listing what it taught them 😬

In reality, the answer that gets in is built on a specific role you actually play, and what it taught you about belonging.

Here’s why each response got its result:
❌ Rejected: Names a broad community (my school, my town) and lists values like teamwork and leadership. There’s no personal role in it, so the same lines could belong to anyone.

⚠️ Waitlisted: Names a real role like volunteer, leader, or mentor, then summarizes the takeaway (“taught me responsibility”). The reader hears about the growth without ever seeing it happen.

✅ Accepted: Shows a specific, recurring action, why it started, and the exact role it gave the student in that community. The insight about belonging is earned through the scene itself.

How you answer “Why do you want to attend XYZ school?” can make the difference between an acceptance, waitlist, or rejection ⬇️

Here’s how each answer differs:

❌ Rejected: This answer could literally apply to any top school. It’s vague, interchangeable, and focuses only on what the student wants to receive, not what they’ve already built or hope to contribute. 

⚠️ Waitlisted: This one has good intentions but stays broad. It mentions interdisciplinary learning and impact, but it doesn’t anchor those ideas in the student’s lived experiences or name anything uniquely Stanford. 

✅ Accepted: This answer is specific, impact-driven, and future-oriented. It names a real Stanford resource (the Sustainability Accelerator), ties it to the student’s past work, and shows how Stanford directly enables their long-term mission. It reads like someone who understands exactly why Stanford is the right fit, and what they’ll contribute back.

When answering school-specific questions, the best thing you can do is connect the school to something you’ve already done, and highlight how a real opportunity directly accelerates the impact you’re trying to make — especially in your own community.

It’s actually REALLY easy to improve your SAT score if you know the right strategies. 

Here are my Top 5:

1. Craft Your Own Precise Answer (COPA) – Reading:
Instead of jumping straight into the answer choices, first write down your own answer on scratch paper after reading the passage. This keeps you focused on what the text actually says and stops you from getting swayed by tempting-but-wrong options.
Example: If a passage says a new school design improves learning, your COPA might be: “innovative = good.”

2. Plug In Numbers (PIN) – Math:
When a question feels abstract with lots of variables, just plug in your own simple numbers (like 2 or 3) to make it concrete.
Example: If a question has variables like x and y, pick x = 2 and see which answer works. You’ll usually get to the right answer faster than solving the whole equation algebraically.

3. Don’t Trust Your Ear – Writing:
The SAT is full of answers that are grammatically wrong but feel natural in conversation. Instead, focus on actual grammar rules like subject-verb agreement, idioms, or pronoun use.
Example: “Each of the players are…” sounds okay, but it should be “Each of the players is…” because “each” is singular.

4. First Read the Question – Reading:
Before diving into a passage, read the question first. That way, you know exactly what to look for and can avoid wasting time trying to understand everything.
Example: If the question asks about the author’s tone, you’re now reading with tone in mind, not trying to remember every fact.

5. Ignore Prepositional Phrases – Writing:
To spot grammar errors faster, mentally cross out prepositional phrases (like “of the students” or “with the red hat”). These phrases often get in the way of identifying the true subject and verb of a sentence.
Example: In “The group of students are excited,” it seems like “students” is the subject but it’s actually “group,” so the correct verb is “is.”

Of course, these are just a few of the many strategies you need to learn…

Day 7 - Map the test 🗺️ 
List every topic that could be tested and label each as weak, medium, or strong.

Day 6 - Micro-recall 🧠 
Quiz yourself on definitions, formulas, and core ideas using look-cover-say

Day 5 - Teach-back 🎙️ 
Explain each topic out loud in simple language until it makes sense without notes.

Day 4 - Guided practice 🧩 
Solve easy-to-medium problems with notes while explaining why each step works. 

Day 3 - Mixed practice 🔀
Practice mixed topics without notes to force retrieval and concept switching.

Day 2 - Exam simulation ⏰ 
Take a timed, no-notes practice set and immediately review every mistake.

Day 1 - Lock In & sleep 😴 
Review only mistakes, stop studying by 7PM, and get a full eight hours of sleep.

The BIGGEST study mistake students make is thinking more hours equals a higher SAT score…

This isn’t true, especially if you’re not using the right strategies. 

I’m a current Harvard student and when I learned how SAT questions are designed, I used strategies that actually took into account the design…

And that’s how I went from a 1270 to 1580. 

Here are my Top 5 strategies: 

1️⃣ The COPA Filter: This stands for Craft (Your) Own Precise Answer. 
1. Read the question. 
2. Read the passage. 
3. Write a short answer in your own words. 
4. Pick the choice that matches yours best.

2️⃣ The TAC Table Trick: This is for any question with a table or chart. 
1. Skip the answer choices
2. Pick one row of real data from the table
3. Plug those values into the equation
4. See what makes sense
5. Then check which answer matches

3️⃣ PIN Hack: When you see a variable, don’t solve it. Just plug in a simple number like 2.
Test each answer with that number. The one that works is your answer.

4️⃣ The 4Q Reading Order: Read in this exact order: Question - Blurb - Passage - Answers. For example, if question asks about tone, you’ll read with emotional words in mind like “frustrated” or “excited.”

5️⃣ Strip to Core Strategy: Cross out all the extra words. For example, “The report from the manager on the desk was confusing” becomes “The report was confusing.” This helps you focus on what matters.

It’s actually REALLY easy to improve your SAT score if you and your friends know the right strategies. 

Here are my Top 5:

1. Craft Your Own Precise Answer (COPA) – Reading:
Instead of jumping straight into the answer choices, first write down your own answer on scratch paper after reading the passage. This keeps you focused on what the text actually says and stops you from getting swayed by tempting-but-wrong options.
Example: If a passage says a new school design improves learning, your COPA might be: “innovative = good.”

2. Plug In Numbers (PIN) – Math:
When a question feels abstract with lots of variables, just plug in your own simple numbers (like 2 or 3) to make it concrete.
Example: If a question has variables like x and y, pick x = 2 and see which answer works. You’ll usually get to the right answer faster than solving the whole equation algebraically.

3. Don’t Trust Your Ear – Writing:
The SAT is full of answers that are grammatically wrong but feel natural in conversation. Instead, focus on actual grammar rules like subject-verb agreement, idioms, or pronoun use.
Example: “Each of the players are…” sounds okay, but it should be “Each of the players is…” because “each” is singular.

4. First Read the Question – Reading:
Before diving into a passage, read the question first. That way, you know exactly what to look for and can avoid wasting time trying to understand everything.
Example: If the question asks about the author’s tone, you’re now reading with tone in mind, not trying to remember every fact.

5. Ignore Prepositional Phrases – Writing:
To spot grammar errors faster, mentally cross out prepositional phrases (like “of the students” or “with the red hat”). These phrases often get in the way of identifying the true subject and verb of a sentence.
Example: In “The group of students are excited,” it seems like “students” is the subject but it’s actually “group,” so the correct verb is “is.”

Of course, these are just a few of the many strategies you need to learn…

Most students think they’re “bad at studying”
when in reality… they were just taught the wrong habits.

Let’s break these down 👇

1. Staying up past 11pm
I know it feels productive. But after ~11pm, your brain is biologically worse at encoding new information. You’re rereading, zoning out, and stealing from tomorrow’s memory by sacrificing sleep. If you don’t remember it the next day, this is why.

2. Rereading the textbook
This is the biggest illusion. Familiarity feels like understanding, but recognition ≠ recall. Your brain gets good at seeing the words, not pulling the ideas out on its own during an exam.

3. Highlighting notes
Highlighting feels organized, not effective. It’s a passive task, which means your brain isn’t being forced to retrieve, struggle, or decide what actually matters. Pretty notes don’t create strong memory pathways.

4. Studying with your phone nearby
Whether your phone is face-up or on silent, your brain is still allocating attention to the possibility of a notification. That constant background distraction lowers focus and slows learning way more than people realize.

5. Watching YouTube videos
Videos make things feel clear while you’re watching. But clarity from someone else explaining ≠ you being able to explain it yourself. If you haven’t paused and tried to recall or solve it alone, you won’t remember most of it.

Study tips that ACTUALLY work incorporate both active recall and metacognition, such as the 20-70-10 Review System and The 3-Layer Build that I explained in past videos…

I’ve read hundreds of personal statements at this point…

The personal statements that stand out usually have four very specific elements: 

1️⃣ First, the opening starts with a real habit or behavior, not a theme. Instead of telling me you care about language, leadership, or growth, it shows me something you actually do repeatedly in your life.

2️⃣ Second, by around 150–200 words, there’s clear tension. Without it, the essay usually reads like a reflection with no story.

3️⃣ Third, the turning point isn’t always a win. In strong essays, it’s the moment where the student isn’t sure if they’re doing the right thing yet. Maybe they’re helping someone and feeling conflicted about it, or realizing that something they thought was positive has a cost.

4️⃣ Finally, strong conclusions are short and grounded, and they show how the student now views the same situation differently than they did at the beginning.

There isn’t a perfect topic for a personal statement. What matters is how specific you get and how clearly your thinking has changed.

Yesterday, I asked my sister how much she studies at UT Austin and was surprised she studies way more than I do at Harvard.

When we talked it through, we realized it wasn’t wasn’t about how hard our classes were…

We were using completely different study strategies.

Here’s the one I use that helps information stick immediately instead of cramming: 

🌟The Blur Test + Immediate Retrieval Loop 🌟

Step 1: Study normally for 20–30 minutes.
Take notes, watch lectures, whatever you usually do.

Step 2: Blur the material. Close your laptop, and flip your notes over. You shouldn’t be able to see anything.

Step 3: Do a full memory dump.
On a blank page, write everything you remember— concepts, formulas, examples, diagrams.

Step 4: Patch only the gaps.
Check your notes and add only what you missed or misunderstood. No rewriting.

Step 5: Loop once more the same day.
Repeat the blur + memory dump later that day to lock it in fast.

Most students reread and feel productive.
This forces recall, which is what actually builds memory.

Practice mixed topics without notes to force retrieval and concept switching.

Take a timed, no-notes practice set and immediately review every mistake.

I used to think getting a higher GPA just meant studying longer. 

But the older I got, the more I realized that most students aren’t struggling because they’re “lazy” or “not smart enough.” 

They’re struggling because no one ever taught them how to study in a way their brain actually responds to.

The difference between a 3.6, a 3.8, and a 4.0 student is almost never effort.
It’s usually STRUCTURE.

One of the methods that helped me the most at Harvard is something I call the 20–5 method:

1️⃣ Choose one clear objective for your 20-minute block. Example:
– Understand how the Krebs cycle produces ATP
– Rework 4 practice problems
– Memorize the steps of a lab technique

2️⃣ Study for 20 minutes with everything open.
Notes, textbook, slides…whatever you need. This is your input phase.

3️⃣ Then 5 minutes of closed-book recall. Try to remember:
– What did I just learn?
– Can I explain it in my own words?
– Could I teach the main idea to someone else?
– What pieces did I forget?

Those five minutes matter more than the twenty. This is where your brain actually strengthens the memory. 

4️⃣ Repeat the cycle a few times, then rest.
What ends up happening is that you cover more in less time, and you retain it longer.

Most high schoolers never get research opportunities because they email one professor, get ignored, and assume they’re “not qualified.”

The Ladder Method has been proven to completely change that for THOUSANDS of high school students. 

Here’s how it works:

1️⃣ Start at the bottom of the ladder.
Begin with grad students, postdocs, or research assistants. They reply far more often because they aren’t flooded with undergrad requests, and they’re the ones actually running the day-to-day experiments.

2️⃣ Move one rung up.
Once a grad student replies, ask whether their PI (the professor) takes high school students or if they’d recommend someone in the department. You’re using their credibility to get upstream access.

3️⃣ Climb to the top.
Now email the professor referencing the name of the person who directed you to them. This single line boosts your response rate more than anything else because no professor ignores someone vetted by their own team.

4️⃣ Close with a tiny ask.
Don’t ask for a job. Ask for one 10-minute call to learn about their work. Come to the call with questions to show genuine curiosity, and pitch at the end. This steps is what maximizes chances at lab positions, research program nominations, and summer opportunities.

Students who use this method stop competing for “posted internships” and start getting opportunities through direct mentorship, which is how most real research pathways work.

If you only want one study technique that actually saves time, this is it 👇

Most people waste hours reviewing everything for exams. 

I used to be like that too…until I discovered the 20–70-10 Review System that I now use before every exam at Harvard.

This system forces you to review ONLY what predicts your grade.

Here’s the exact framework:

🧩 STEP 1 — The 20% (Input Pass)
- Skim the chapter/notes once
- Highlight ONLY these:
 • Definitions
 • Equations
 • “Why/How” explanations
- Turn each highlight into a question (5–10 total)

🧪 STEP 2 — The 70% (Output Pass)
- Answer every question from memory
-  If you miss one, write:
 • What I thought it was
 • What it actually is
 • Why I confused it
- Add the missed items to a running list called “Exam Triggers”

🧠 STEP 3 — The 10% (Targeted Fix)
- Review ONLY the Exam Triggers
- Turn each trigger into one flashcard or one practice problem
- Redo the Output Pass on just those

This saves time because you do one light input pass…
then spend 70% of your time on output (what exams actually test)…
then fix ONLY your blindspots.

I’m a current Harvard student and what actually changed my GPA was understanding the science behind why these habits don’t work:

❌ Re-reading the textbook
❌ Highlighting everything
❌ Memorizing flashcards in the same order

These fall into the familiarity trap. Your brain recognizes the information, but it cannot recall it under pressure, which is why so many students blank on exams.

✅ What actually works is an active recall technique called The 3 Layer Build:

1️⃣ Outline Layer: Write the topic at the top of a blank page. Add 3 to 5 bullet points you remember without notes.

2️⃣ Explain Layer: Choose one point and explain it in simple language, like you’re teaching a confused friend. Getting stuck shows you what to review.

3️⃣ Application Layer: Create one new example or practice problem using the idea in a different way. Solve it or explain it to build flexible recall.

In high school, everyone told me that highlighting and rewriting my notes was “the most effective way to study”

But I kept burning myself out spending hours “studying” only to forget them once I opened my exam. 

Once I got to Harvard, I was taught the Compression–Expansion Loop.

It’s one of the most effective study methods that forces your brain to store and recall information with minimal time and effort. 

Here’s how it works 👇
1️⃣ Compression: After you study something, summarize it into 2–3 short sentences or one simple diagram. (Basically “zip” the info into its core idea.)

2️⃣ Expansion: A few hours or days later, try to rebuild the full explanation or process from memory (no notes or textbook)

If you can expand it clearly, you actually understand it.

If you can’t, you know exactly what to review.

It’s how a lot of Harvard students handle insane amounts of material because trains their recall.

Most students think better grades = more study time.
But I got top exam scores by studying less.

Here’s how I stopped overstudying and started outscoring everyone around me without pulling all-nighters or giving up my free time.

4 hacks that helped me ace exams without studying more:

🧠 Hack #1: The Blur Test
→ Instead of rereading notes, I’d glance at a page for 15 seconds, blur my eyes, and try to recall everything I just saw.
→ Forces active recall, not passive review… and you’ll retain 2x more in half the time.

🧠 Hack #2: The 80/20 Focus Rule
→ I identified the 20% of material that showed up on 80% of past exams.
→ I didn’t treat everything equally, but I went deep with the core concepts and ignored all the extra details. 

🧠 Hack #3: “Teach It Ugly”
→ I explained confusing topics out loud to a pretend audience like I was a chaotic YouTuber.
→ Teaching without notes helped me remember 10x more than silent review ever did.

🧠 Hack #4: 1-Minute Recap Ritual
→ After each class, I’d spend one minute writing the 3 biggest takeaways from memory.
→ That tiny habit trained my brain to encode faster so I didn’t need to “relearn” it all before the exam.

These micro-changes helped me study less, learn faster, and finally breathe again during finals season.

Most students don’t actually know how to study. I didn’t either.

At 16, I was constantly behind even though I was working harder than everyone around me. 

These 4 study hacks changed everything for me:

🧠 Hack #1: The 3-Sentence Fix
→  After every mistake on homework or practice tests, I forced myself to write 3 sentences:
	1.	What I did wrong
	2.	What the correct approach was
	3.	What I’ll do differently next time
→  This helped me stop repeating the same mistakes and sharpened my ability to recognize patterns across subjects.

 🧠 Hack #2: Spaced Priming
→ Before each class, I would glance through the lecture slides or textbook for just 5 minutes.
→ I wasn’t trying to understand everything. I was simply flagging ideas as “important” so when I heard them in class, my brain clicked faster.
→  That reduced how much I needed to study after school.

 🧠 Hack #3: Cognitive Closure Loop
→ Every night before bed, I would write down the questions I was stuck on during the day without trying to solve them.
→ This gave my brain permission to rest and reset instead of obsessing over what I didn’t understand.
→ The next day, I found myself more focused and ready to work through those gaps.

 🧠 Hack #4: Contextual Review
→ Instead of always reviewing in the same spot, I rotated between 2 or 3 different locations like my desk, the kitchen table, even my backyard.
→ Seeing the same material in different environments helped me remember it longer because I wasn’t relying on location-based memory.

These small changes helped me stop overstudying and finally start learning efficiently.

 🧠 Hack #3: Cognitive Closure Loop
→ Every night before bed, I would write down the questions I was stuck on during the day without trying to solve them.
→ This gave my brain permission to rest and reset instead of obsessing over what I didn’t understand.
→ The next day, I found myself more focused and ready to work through those gaps.

 🧠 Hack #4: Contextual Review
→ Instead of always reviewing in the same spot, I rotated between 2 or 3 different locations like my desk, the kitchen table, even my backyard.
→ Seeing the same material in different environments helped me remember it longer because I wasn’t relying on location-based memory.

It’s actually REALLY easy to improve your SAT score if you know the right strategies. 

Here are my Top 5:

1. Craft Your Own Precise Answer (COPA) – Reading:
Instead of jumping straight into the answer choices, first write down your own answer on scratch paper after reading the passage. This keeps you focused on what the text actually says and stops you from getting swayed by tempting-but-wrong options.
Example: If a passage says a new school design improves learning, your COPA might be: “innovative = good.”

2. Plug In Numbers (PIN) – Math:
When a question feels abstract with lots of variables, just plug in your own simple numbers (like 2 or 3) to make it concrete.
Example: If a question has variables like x and y, pick x = 2 and see which answer works. You’ll usually get to the right answer faster than solving the whole equation algebraically.

3. Don’t Trust Your Ear – Writing:
The SAT is full of answers that are grammatically wrong but feel natural in conversation. Instead, focus on actual grammar rules like subject-verb agreement, idioms, or pronoun use.
Example: “Each of the players are…” sounds okay, but it should be “Each of the players is…” because “each” is singular.

4. First Read the Question – Reading:
Before diving into a passage, read the question first. That way, you know exactly what to look for and can avoid wasting time trying to understand everything.
Example: If the question asks about the author’s tone, you’re now reading with tone in mind, not trying to remember every fact.

5. Ignore Prepositional Phrases – Writing:
To spot grammar errors faster, mentally cross out prepositional phrases (like “of the students” or “with the red hat”). These phrases often get in the way of identifying the true subject and verb of a sentence.
Example: In “The group of students are excited,” it seems like “students” is the subject but it’s actually “group,” so the correct verb is “is.”

Of course, these are just a few of the many strategies you need to learn…

Why is it so important to familiarize with concepts before you walk into class?

This technique is called priming 🧠

When your teacher presents you with details, your brain tends to fill in gaps of the bigger picture. 

If you have a general idea of the concept, you’ll form neural connections quicker 🖇️

The reality of common habits 🧠⬇️ 

1. Re-writing your notes

- Note-taking is a passive action that creates an illusion of productivity. In reality, testing your ability to recall information is the key to forming neural connections. 

2. Re-reading your textbook

- Avoid doing this as your main method of studying for an exam. It’s a low-utility action that doesn’t allow you to discover your knowledge gaps. 

3. Pulling all-nighters

- Deep rest builds neuroplasticity. Despite studying hard, if you don’t sleep enough, your ability to memorize information long-term is reduced. 

4. Ignoring your biological cycle

- Everyone’s peak productivity time differs. Identify yours and set aside that period of time for intense study sessions. Trying to study hard when your body isn’t at its peak leads to unproductive work.
